children: One of the last century's most reliable trading strategies no longer seems to work. A new study has found a way to resurrect it.

I'm referring to what's known as the "short-term reversal effect," or Strev, which is the tendency for stocks that have performed the best over a given month to be losers in the subsequent month, and vice versa.

For decades, short-term traders relied on this tendency to rack up impressive gains, buying those stocks that lost the most in the prior month and shorting — that is, betting they would fall in value — those that made the most. As you can see from the accompanying chart, which plots the Strev's trailing five-year profitability, in recent years the strategy has been a loser.

Also relevant is the dismal performance of an exchange-traded fund that was created to exploit this effect. Between its launch in September 2018 to when it was closed in March 2025, the Vesper US Large Cap Short Term Reversal Strategy ETF underperformed the S&P 500 index by 3.8 annualized percentage points, according to LSEG data.

The new study, "Asymmetric Reversals," began circulating in academic circles. It was written by Federico Baldi-Lanfranchi of the Lake Lucerne Institute, Pierre Collin-Dufresne of the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne — and Kent Daniel of Columbia University's Business School, formerly Goldman Sachs' co-chief investment officer.

The researchers found that two factors are reducing the Strev's profitability. The first is that some of the stocks with big gains or losses in a given month don't reverse themselves in the subsequent one, but instead continue moving in the same direction. These stocks tend to be those whose big moves in the first month were "justified" — in the sense that there was a plausible rationale for why they moved as much as they did. The second factor is that large short-term losses reverse themselves much more quickly (typically in two weeks or less) than large short-term gains (typically over a couple of months).

To properly exploit the Strev, therefore, traders need to focus only on stocks for which there is no rationale for their big moves over the prior month, and refresh the long side of their portfolio far more often than the short side — by selling the stocks held long more frequently and replacing them with a new set of stocks that have lost the most over the prior month.
The researchers found the Strev's profitability grew dramatically upon doing both of these things.

Following the first half of this advice might seem to be a tall order. But the researchers found a way, by constructing a complex econometric model out of dozens of individual indicators that prior research has found to have explanatory value. If that model could explain why a given stock moved up or down in a big way, it was put into the category of those whose moves were "justified." Traders trying to exploit the Strev should avoid those stocks and focus instead on those for which no rationale can be found.

Don't panic. You don't need to employ the researchers' complex econometric model to exploit this new study's findings, Daniel said in an interview. That's because there are several back-of-the-envelope calculations you can make that do at least a creditable job of identifying those stocks that are more likely to reverse. He added that an intelligent and careful use of artificial intelligence might be able to make these calculations for you, though he and his co-authors have not investigated that possibility.

Regardless of whether you use AI or do the calculations yourself, the key is to focus on factors such as whether the stock's company had announced unexpectedly good or bad news, or whether the other stocks in the same industry also made a similarly sized move. If either of these things is the case, then the stock in question won't reverse its prior month move, on average.

Daniel stresses that exploiting the Strev requires building a diversified portfolio of stocks on both the long and short sides. That's because the odds of a reversal in the case of any one individual stock are relatively modest. Only when owning a well-diversified portfolio of reversal candidates do the odds improve to very much in your favor. (To sell a stock short, of course, you borrow shares of that stock from your broker and sell them. If the stock's price falls, you realize a profit when repaying your broker.)

There are other ways of exploiting the researchers' revised Strev, however. One is by narrowing the focus of momentum strategies, which buy stocks that have performed the best over the prior year and short those that have lost the most. Because of the Strev, momentum traders traditionally have ignored the most recent month when determining which stocks to buy or sell.

The implication of this new study is that your profit may increase by focusing on the full trailing 12-month return of stocks for which plausible rationales can be found for big prior-month moves, buying those with the best returns and shorting those with the worst.

Another way of exploiting this new study is when you are buying or selling stocks for other reasons. It behooves you in that case to determine if your buy or sell candidates have made a big move over the prior month and if plausible rationales exist for those moves. If those rationales can be found, you should expect them to continue moving in the same direction in the weeks after you buy or sell. Otherwise, just the opposite would be the case.
